newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban seek U.N. help, but harrass U.N. staff.
newsitem.headline: Taleban seek U.N. help, but harrass U.N. staff.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban movement has asked the United Nations for help in brokering peace and rebuilding the war-shattered country, but tension is mounting between the Taleban and U.N. staff on the ground.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) this week put most of its activities in Kabul on hold until security improves for its local staff, four of whom have been detained and seven, who are women, told to stay at home.

Taleban-controlled Sharia radio said on Thursday that Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Stanakzai had told a U.N. official that some local UNHCR employees had used the agency's radio to pass military information to opposition forces.
Mullah Wakil Ahmad, a Taleban spokesman in the southern city of Kandahar, urged the UNHCR to resume its activities and said the Taleban government would protect UNHCR establishments.

"The UNHCR is more than ready and willing to carry out is programmes in Kabul, where they are badly needed," UNHCR spokesman Rupert Colville said on Friday. "But we still need the basic security conditions in which to operate."

Relations have been difficult between the Taleban, who seized Kabul on September 27 as part of a drive to spread strict Islamic sharia law across the country, and foreign aid workers and journalists used to the easier-going attitudes of the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Aid agencies have had to cope with Taleban strictures on the mixing of sexes in work and education. Some, like Save the Children, are unable to operate without their women staff.
Others, trying to carry on, faced threats to their Afghan women employees and arrests of some of their male staff members, with those of Tajik or Uzbek ethnic origin apparently singled out.
A foreign staff member of the International Committee of the Red Cross was beaten and held overnight for breaking the curfew.

Foreign reporters have also found life harder under the Taleban. Visiting journalists have been forced to stay at the grim, rocket-scarred Continental Hotel, where they are pressed to use only hotel drivers and take Taleban "minders" with them.
"We have enforced Islamic principles for the men and women of Afghanistan and the United Nations has no right to argue with them," Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said on Thursday.

"In general we are very happy with the activities of the U.N. Our only complaint is that they lack understanding of Afghanistan and Afghan society. We hope that they don't make the mistake of comparing Afghan society to Western society."

Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous said in a letter this week to U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, "We do not represent an extremist or militant force as has been suggested and portrayed by certain external quarters."

"We deeply regret that forces inimical to the unity and peace in Afghanistan have continued to present a completely distorted picture of our policies and approach to redressing the socio-economic problems of Afghanistan," he wrote.

Ghous pledged full support for U.N. peace efforts in the letter, timed to coincide with Monday's meeting on Afghanistan at the United Nations. The Taleban had previously criticised the meeting as "useless" because no Afghan factions were invited.
Apart from complaining about the Taleban's "distorted" image abroad, Ghous set out peace proposals broadly similar to those of an opposition alliance that includes the former government.

Rabbani said in Paris on Thursday his forces did not plan to re-take Kabul by force and urged the Taleban to negotiate a ceasefire. "We have proposed to the Taleban and the United Nations that Kabul be declared an open and demilitarised city."
Both sides agree on the need for a ceasefire and a political dialogue that would focus on demilitarisation of Kabul and creation of a neutral security force, but not on the details.

"It is imperative that the international community rededicate itself to promoting peace and unity of Afghanistan, which is vital for the stability of our volatile region," Ghous wrote in his letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
"It is imperative that the needs of the Afghan people be met through a well-coordinated programme of humanitarian assistance," he wrote.
Foreign aid workers say the Taleban must adjust their behaviour if they want help from the outside world.
"The reality is that many agencies are suffering from an unhealthy climate of suspicion and tension and cannot function in those conditions," said one U.N. official privately.
